raw_evidence.label: The shape of laughter: long tail
raw_evidence.content: The distribution of laugh durations is sharply long-tailed. 573 of 925 captions get no laugh at all. Among lines that do trigger laughter, most are short — 41 sit at 0.5s, 47 at 1.0s, 34 at 1.5s. As you move out into the longer durations the counts collapse: only 28 captions hit 5 seconds or more, only 11 reach 7 seconds, only 4 reach 8 seconds, and exactly one reaches 10 seconds. Comedy on this evidence is not a steady stream of equally funny moments — it is a baseline of small smiles punctuated by a handful of rare detonations.

print(f"\nMax: {max(c['laugh'] for c in captions)}")

print(f"Captions with laugh >= 6s: {sum(1 for c in captions if c['laugh'] >= 6)}")
print(f"Captions with laugh >= 7s: {sum(1 for c in captions if c['laugh'] >= 7)}")

print(f"Captions with laugh >= 10s: {sum(1 for c in captions if c['laugh'] >= 10)}")

print("Minute, laugh_seconds")

Among lines that do trigger laughter, most are short — 41 sit at 0.5s, 47 at 1.0s, 34 at 1.5s. raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: laughter as the only ground truth
raw_evidence.content: Caption-level laughter duration is an unusual quantitative signal. Most analyses of comedy text are about word choice, timing, or rhythm; here the audience's reaction is measured in seconds and attached to the exact line that triggered it. That gives us a direct dependent variable. But two confounds deserve a flag for the analyst. First, laughter is contagious and lagged — the seconds tagged to a caption are partly a reaction to *that* line and partly tail-off from the previous beat. Second, the laughter values are quantized in coarse units (whole and half seconds) by hand, so very small differences should not be over-interpreted. The headline patterns — biggest single laugh, distribution shape, where laughter clusters — are robust to both confounds.

raw_evidence.label: Background: what a callback is
raw_evidence.content: A callback is a structural device in stand-up: the comic refers to material established earlier in the same set and recontextualizes it for a new laugh. Callbacks are not simple repetitions — they must work as a fresh joke and reward the audience for having paid attention. Practitioners describe two effects that matter for The Pudding's argument. First, callbacks make a long set feel less like a list and more like a single connected piece of writing. Second, distance matters: a callback that arrives a few seconds later feels like part of the original beat, while a callback that arrives many minutes later operates more like a surprise reveal, because the audience has half-forgotten the seed. In Wong's special, the topics CSV records three explicit callbacks (rows where the `callback` column points back to a prior topic's start time), so the dataset lets us see this technique used at long range.

raw_evidence.label: Why it matters: what the original Pudding piece argued
raw_evidence.content: The original Pudding essay argues that stand-up exists on a spectrum from one-liners (Mitch Hedberg) to fully narrative, structurally interconnected routines, and that Ali Wong's special sits far down the structural end. Their core claim — and the reason this dataset is useful — is that Wong's biggest laugh, the 'laughter climax', does not get its size from the punchline alone. It gets its size because by that moment the audience is holding several earlier topics in their head simultaneously, and the joke ties them together. The dataset lets readers test this claim: each caption row carries a measured laughter duration in seconds, and the topics CSV records when one bit calls back to another. We can therefore line up the moments where structure converges with the moments where the audience laughed hardest.

raw_evidence.label: Topic structure: a six-level nest
raw_evidence.content: Wong's set is unusually deep structurally. The annotators recorded 131 topics arranged across 6 nesting levels — 10 at the top, 21 at level 2, 43 at level 3 (the most populated level), 31 at level 4, 19 at level 5, and 7 at level 6. Most stand-up sets are flat lists of bits; this one branches like a tree, with sub-topics sprouting from sub-topics. Level 3 is the workhorse — that's where most of the actual content lives. Levels 4-6 are deep digressions that, structurally, are children of children of children of one of the ten top-level chapters.

raw_evidence.label: Background: what a callback is
raw_evidence.content: A callback is a structural device in stand-up: the comic refers to material established earlier in the same set and recontextualizes it for a new laugh. Callbacks are not simple repetitions — they must work as a fresh joke and reward the audience for having paid attention. Practitioners describe two effects that matter for The Pudding's argument. First, callbacks make a long set feel less like a list and more like a single connected piece of writing. Second, distance matters: a callback that arrives a few seconds later feels like part of the original beat, while a callback that arrives many minutes later operates more like a surprise reveal, because the audience has half-forgotten the seed. In Wong's special, the topics CSV records three explicit callbacks (rows where the `callback` column points back to a prior topic's start time), so the dataset lets us see this technique used at long range.

In Wong's special, the topics CSV records three explicit callbacks (rows where the `callback` column points back to a prior topic's start time), so the dataset lets us see this technique used at long range.

raw_evidence.label: Deeper bits get bigger laughs
raw_evidence.content: When you bucket every caption by the nesting level of the topic it lives in, average laughter rises with depth — and so do the maximums. Level-1 captions average 0.57s of laughter; level 4 averages 0.90s and contains the only 10-second laugh in the set. Levels 5 and 6 average 0.97s and 0.87s. Level 1 and 2 captions are mostly chapter introductions ('let's talk about marriage', 'let's talk about pregnancy') that exist to set up later bits, not to be funny themselves. The further Wong burrows down a digression, the harder the audience laughs at what she finds. This is the dataset's clearest endorsement of The Pudding's structural argument: payoff tracks depth.

raw_evidence.label: Why it matters: what the original Pudding piece argued
raw_evidence.content: The original Pudding essay argues that stand-up exists on a spectrum from one-liners (Mitch Hedberg) to fully narrative, structurally interconnected routines, and that Ali Wong's special sits far down the structural end. Their core claim — and the reason this dataset is useful — is that Wong's biggest laugh, the 'laughter climax', does not get its size from the punchline alone. It gets its size because by that moment the audience is holding several earlier topics in their head simultaneously, and the joke ties them together. The dataset lets readers test this claim: each caption row carries a measured laughter duration in seconds, and the topics CSV records when one bit calls back to another. We can therefore line up the moments where structure converges with the moments where the audience laughed hardest.

sentences.summary: det_03: Background: what a callback is. Source: Callback (comedy) — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callback_(comedy)) Facts: A callback is a joke that refers to one previously told in the set.; It must be structured as a new joke, not a repetition. Source: Callback Comedy: How to Perform and Write Callbacks — Backstage (https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/callback-comedy-explained-76712/) Facts: Callbacks recontextualize earlier material for a new laugh.; Distance between setup and callback affects comedic impact.

raw_evidence.label: Background: what a callback is
raw_evidence.content: A callback is a structural device in stand-up: the comic refers to material established earlier in the same set and recontextualizes it for a new laugh. Callbacks are not simple repetitions — they must work as a fresh joke and reward the audience for having paid attention. Practitioners describe two effects that matter for The Pudding's argument. First, callbacks make a long set feel less like a list and more like a single connected piece of writing. Second, distance matters: a callback that arrives a few seconds later feels like part of the original beat, while a callback that arrives many minutes later operates more like a surprise reveal, because the audience has half-forgotten the seed. In Wong's special, the topics CSV records three explicit callbacks (rows where the `callback` column points back to a prior topic's start time), so the dataset lets us see this technique used at long range.

raw_evidence.label: Three callbacks — and they reach back further than you'd expect
raw_evidence.content: The topics CSV records exactly three explicit callbacks. The shortest reach-back is still 12 minutes 24 seconds; the longest is 46 minutes 11 seconds. The first ('When I pee, I need to see ten gallons of bleach' → hippies routine, fired at 49:43) reaches back 33 minutes. The second ('blaming mom' → 'told my mom from a third world country', fired at 50:57) reaches back 46 minutes — across nearly the entire special. The third (the 'wet' callback at 56:48 referencing a 'wet' beat at 44:24) reaches back 12 minutes. Distance between setup and callback is enormous: in two of three cases the seed was planted in the first ten minutes of the show and harvested in the last ten.
raw_evidence.code:
chap_laugh = sum(c["laugh"] for c in captions
                     if c["timeStart"] >= t["timeStart"] and c["timeStart"] < t["topicEnd"])
    chap_caps = [c for c in captions
                 if c["timeStart"] >= t["timeStart"] and c["timeStart"] < t["topicEnd"]]
    talk_secs = sum(c["timeStop"] - c["timeStart"] for c in chap_caps)
    print(f"  {t['group']:25s}  {fmt_mmss(t['timeStart'])}–{fmt_mmss(t['topicEnd'])}  "
          f"span={span}s  laugh={chap_laugh:.1f}s  ({chap_laugh/span*100:.1f}% of chapter)")

# --- ana_13: Properly resolved callbacks ---
print("\n=== ana_13 ===")
# Find the topic whose timeStart equals the callback's seconds (some are nested children)
print("Callback resolution (nearest topic at-or-before target time):")
all_t_start = sorted(((t["timeStart"], t["group"]) for t in topics if t["timeStart"] is not None),
                     key=lambda x: x[0])
for t in topics:
    if t["callback_seconds"] is None:
        continue
    target = t["callback_seconds"]
    # find the topic whose timeStart is closest at-or-before target
    best = None
    for ts, g in all_t_start:
        if ts <= target:
            best = (ts, g)
        else:
            break
    distance = t["timeStart"] - target
    # find caption text closest to the target time, for human-readable label
    nearby_target_caps = [c for c in captions if abs(c["timeStart"] - target) < 30]
raw_evidence.output:

Callback at 56:48 (896-wet) → target topic at 44:24 (697-wet); reach back: 744s (12m 24s)

raw_evidence.label: Why it matters: what the original Pudding piece argued
raw_evidence.content: The original Pudding essay argues that stand-up exists on a spectrum from one-liners (Mitch Hedberg) to fully narrative, structurally interconnected routines, and that Ali Wong's special sits far down the structural end. Their core claim — and the reason this dataset is useful — is that Wong's biggest laugh, the 'laughter climax', does not get its size from the punchline alone. It gets its size because by that moment the audience is holding several earlier topics in their head simultaneously, and the joke ties them together. The dataset lets readers test this claim: each caption row carries a measured laughter duration in seconds, and the topics CSV records when one bit calls back to another. We can therefore line up the moments where structure converges with the moments where the audience laughed hardest.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook: laughter as the only ground truth
raw_evidence.content: Caption-level laughter duration is an unusual quantitative signal. Most analyses of comedy text are about word choice, timing, or rhythm; here the audience's reaction is measured in seconds and attached to the exact line that triggered it. That gives us a direct dependent variable. But two confounds deserve a flag for the analyst. First, laughter is contagious and lagged — the seconds tagged to a caption are partly a reaction to *that* line and partly tail-off from the previous beat. Second, the laughter values are quantized in coarse units (whole and half seconds) by hand, so very small differences should not be over-interpreted. The headline patterns — biggest single laugh, distribution shape, where laughter clusters — are robust to both confounds.

raw_evidence.label: The shape of laughter: long tail
raw_evidence.content: The distribution of laugh durations is sharply long-tailed. 573 of 925 captions get no laugh at all. Among lines that do trigger laughter, most are short — 41 sit at 0.5s, 47 at 1.0s, 34 at 1.5s. As you move out into the longer durations the counts collapse: only 28 captions hit 5 seconds or more, only 11 reach 7 seconds, only 4 reach 8 seconds, and exactly one reaches 10 seconds. Comedy on this evidence is not a steady stream of equally funny moments — it is a baseline of small smiles punctuated by a handful of rare detonations.
raw_evidence.code:
hist = []
for (lo, hi), lbl in zip(buckets, labels):
    n = sum(1 for c in captions if lo <= c["laugh"] <= hi)
    hist.append((lbl, n))
    print(f"  {lbl:8s}  {n:4d}")
print(f"\nMax: {max(c['laugh'] for c in captions)}")
print(f"Captions with laugh >= 5s: {sum(1 for c in captions if c['laugh'] >= 5)}")
print(f"Captions with laugh >= 6s: {sum(1 for c in captions if c['laugh'] >= 6)}")
print(f"Captions with laugh >= 7s: {sum(1 for c in captions if c['laugh'] >= 7)}")
print(f"Captions with laugh >= 8s: {sum(1 for c in captions if c['laugh'] >= 8)}")
print(f"Captions with laugh >= 10s: {sum(1 for c in captions if c['laugh'] >= 10)}")

# --- ana_04: Laughter-by-minute (rolling profile of the hour) ---
print("\n=== ana_04 ===")
minute_laugh = [0.0] * 60
for c in captions:
    m = c["timeStart"] // 60
    if m < 60:
        minute_laugh[m] += c["laugh"]
print("Minute, laugh_seconds")
for m, v in enumerate(minute_laugh):
    print(f"  {m:2d}  {v:.1f}")
peak_min = minute_laugh.index(max(minute_laugh))
print(f"\nPeak minute: {peak_min} ({minute_laugh[peak_min]:.1f} s of laughter)")

raw_evidence.content: The original Pudding essay argues that stand-up exists on a spectrum from one-liners (Mitch Hedberg) to fully narrative, structurally interconnected routines, and that Ali Wong's special sits far down the structural end. It gets its size because by that moment the audience is holding several earlier topics in their head simultaneously, and the joke ties them together. The dataset lets readers test this claim: each caption row carries a measured laughter duration in seconds, and the topics CSV records when one bit calls back to another. We can therefore line up the moments where structure converges with the moments where the audience laughed hardest.
